### scene-card  <novel/chapters/ch-01/chapter.yaml>

Scene s-001. Intent: Open the novel on the transaction: Rue's decision to sell herself and sign the Contract. Establish the Mercy Academy's public face, the rule that it takes one hundred girls each year, and the notorious statistic that after ten years only three ever walk back out. Introduce the Contract, the Folio and the Headmistress as symbols.

Target length: about 1176 words.

### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

Rue, who sold herself into the Mercy Academy, spends a lifetime inside the institution that annually accepts one hundred girls but returns almost none; when war reaches the Academy's gates in her old age, buried bargains and the Academy's true price are forced into daylight, and Rue must reckon with what she once bargained away.

### entity-roster  <characters/, locations/, objects/>

Every entity that exists in this story. Only these ids may be used; if you need someone or something that is not here, say so rather than inventing an id.
- char-rue: Rue — A woman who sold herself into the Mercy Academy as a young woman. Quiet, practical, and watchful, she spends decades inside the Academy and grows into its reluctant conscience.
- collective-the-hundred: The Hundred — The Academy's annual cohort: one hundred girls acquired each year and folded into its programs. They are both a number and a shifting constellation of friendships, rivalries and losses.
- collective-the-three: The Three — The near-mythic set of alumni who, historically, have left the Academy after ten years. They are spoken of like miracles and warnings at once.
- char-headmistress: Headmistress — The senior administrator and public face of the Mercy Academy. Polished, diplomatic and possessed of practical ruthlessness; she embodies the Academy's benevolent rhetoric and its hard edges.
- char-war-envoy: War Envoy — A representative of the approaching war: formal, implacable and strange. He/they arrive with offers and threats that make the Academy's hidden arrangements surface.
- loc-mercy-academy: Mercy Academy — A high, walled institution on an island quartered between harbor, rose gardens and glasshouses. It calls itself sanctuary and school; its walls hold more than classrooms.
- loc-great-hall: Great Hall — The Academy's ceremonial heart: where the Hundred are received, where names are read into the folio and where the Headmistress meets visitors.
- loc-ink-room: Ink Room — A locked room below the library where the Academy's ledgers and the binding inks are kept. Staffed by a small, generational guild of scribes.
- obj-contract: Contract — The ledger contract each recruit signs. On its face it promises education and safety in return for ten years; its margins hold clauses not printed for patrons.
- obj-folio: Folio — The Academy's ceremonial book that bears the names of every girl who entered and every name that was allowed to leave. It is heavy, stained and glossed with old inks.
- obj-amber-bell: Amber Bell — A small bell rung whenever a cohort is closed or when a departure is recorded in the folio. Its sound is both celebration and seal.
- obj-binding-seal: Binding Seal — A wax-and-ink sigil used in finalizing contracts; it carries a sorcerous tether that makes some of the Academy's claims enforceable.
- char-aya: Aya — A bright, quick-witted recruit in Rue's first cohort at the Academy; she becomes Rue's close friend and an emotional anchor early in Rue's life there.
- char-loren: Loren — An older instructor who teaches craft and discipline to the Hundred. Stern but humane, he mentors Rue across decades and becomes one of the few inside the walls whom she trusts.
- char-elaine: Elaine — One of the named individuals counted among the Three. She left the Academy years ago and lives beyond the city; she carries a scar the Academy never explains.
- char-maris: Maris — Another of the Three. She left under different circumstances and is used by the Academy as an example of success.
- char-sal: Sal — The third of the Three, quieter and more evasive; rumours say she left with secrets the Academy does not want repeated.
- obj-archive-key: Archive Key — A small iron key, stamped with the Academy's crest, used to open the deepest cabinets in the Ink Room and the library's sealed stacks.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- The Academy accepts exactly one hundred girls into a cohort each year; this number is public and rigid in the story's social systems.
- Historically, after a ten-year period inside the Academy, only three individuals have left and their departures are recorded in the Folio (this historical fact is established early and treated as canon unless explicitly changed by a scena-level event with provenance).
- Contracts the recruits sign are legally and magically binding when sealed with the Binding Seal; the Seal enacts the Academy's claims but requires the Academy's own rituals to be maintained.
- Magic has a cost: any enchantment that binds a person's freedom draws from the same ledger as the Folio and must be accounted for in the Academy's records; bargains cannot be silently created or negated without record.
- The War Envoy represents external political/military forces; he may demand terms, levy burdens, or threaten force, but he cannot invent or erase Academy records — only expose and exploit them.
- The Folio truthfully records entries and departures; it can be read and misread, hidden, or weaponised, but altering historical entries is itself an action with consequences and must be shown on-page when it happens.
- The Headmistress is powerful within the Academy but not omnipotent; she must work within political constraints, her staff and the Academy's rituals.
- No deus ex machina: solutions to the Academy's bindings must arise from revealed rules and the characters' established resources and relationships, not from unexplained new powers.

I arrived with my pockets full of nothing and the honest calculation that followed. Two coins would stretch two days at the market; one bed at the lodging house meant a back that never stopped aching and a mouth that never stopped asking. There are neat words for bravery and grander sentences for sacrifice. I had twenty years' worth of sentences inside me. What I had in the moment was hunger and arithmetic. So I sold myself.

The Ceremony Hall smelled of beeswax polish and boiled linen: the kind of clean that announces itself rather than earning quiet trust. Light came through high windows in long, patient bars. The hundred benches were arranged like a small amphitheatre; families sat in the outer rings, sober as undertakers. In the middle, on a low table, lay the Folio and the Contract: the Folio a wide, dark book with a ribbon that had once been more important than it was now; the Contract folded into a small, precise packet, the paper rubbed where hands had touched it for decades.

The Folio was open where a scribe had left it, a pale rectangle of invitation: “Folio Entry — Name: __________________; Age: __; Date: ______; Intake: One hundred; Provenance (sold/placed/orphaned): __________; Signature: __________________; Witness: Headmistress / Scribe.” I read it while they adjusted the sash at the back of my shirt. Reading paperwork is a kind of prayer for people like me.

They called the intake. The Bell — a single bronze note struck from a high arch — cut the murmurs and put us under the House's attention. I counted the sound more as an accountant than a believer: one clear note for the beginning, then the low chorus of the Headmistress's voice as she took the liturgy of charity down the line.

The Headmistress was everything polished with use. She wore mercy as other people wear good coats — tailored to fit, and kept for public weather. Her voice carried over the benches in a soft, precise tide. She read the facts aloud in the way a town clerk reads a deed.

"Out of the hundred who enter each year," she said, "only three leave at the end of their ten-year term. The rest remain under the Academy's charge as is recorded." There was no scolding there, only the small hardness of a truth stated so the room could register it. I had expected myth; I had not expected arithmetic.

When she closed, she laid the policy of the House into a sentence that would follow all our names, and repeated the line that the Folio itself required be heard: "So entered under the charge of the Mercy Academy. Let the Folio stand as record and law. Let those within this house remember that mercy is accounted for by service and attention, not by indulgence." The scribe moved an inkwell with ceremonious care, and the Contract was handed to me.

There are ways to refuse that sound like refusal and ways that are simple. I did not make a show of hesitating. I thought of the lodging house's thin broth, the cough from the woman who shared my bed, the child who asked for a scrap she would not get. I thought of work under a roof that would not change its mind because a winter came early.

The Contract's clause was quiet in the packet but not shy: ten years. The writing named it without flourish — a span not measured in noble phrase but in the clear currency of years. I traced the number with a fingertip as the scribe held the folio steady. Ten years is a ledger entry; it is not a promise of comfort.

I signed in a hand that had practised keeping accounts in cramped ledgers. The pen felt like a small instrument of business. My name was a line, small and tidy. The scribe copied it into the Folio in ink that smelled of iron and permanence. The Headmistress dipped a fingertip and made a mark beside the signature — her witness. The page closed.

There was applause, the kind meant to be mindful. A girl near me cried once, sharp and immediate; nobody shushed her. Mourning and commerce live in the same house and know how to move around one another.

Outside the Hall the sun hit the Academy walls. Inside, the Folio rested where it would be put to the Archive later, an obvious book that contained, in its margins, the small remarks that always get made: nicknames, a note if someone arrived with a child, exceptions the institution had allowed itself. I had read enough of such margins to know that there are things only the Archive says aloud, and only later.

I walked out with a small packet in my palm and a larger accounting on my shoulders. The bargain I had made was practical and unsentimental: room, work, a roof, and ten years of measured claims. The Academy had the language for it all — intake, witness, folio, charge — and I had my signature. I had consented.

Later I would learn the ways the house keeps its numbers neat: how the Folio is consulted when a girl asks to leave, how the ledger rooms hold answer-keys to questions you do not yet have. For now, the decision that mattered was simple and cold as coin: I had fewer options than the day before and one guaranteed where-to-sleep. My humor about it was small and private. I told myself the trade was sensible.

When the bronze note sounded again, it sounded like a clock. The Bell finished the ceremony and put the House back into its ordinary rhythm. I folded the Contract into my pocket the way you fold a receipt for a transaction that you do not plan to return. That night, when I lay in my clean bed for the first time in months, I thought of the Folio's blank lines and the Headmistress's closing line, and I felt the arithmetic of my choice settle down into the room: a tidy sum, a term, and a witness.

./runtime/transcripts/orchestrator/run-2026-07-27T13-32-39-368Z.jsonl:8:{"at":"2026-07-27T13:36:42.197Z","txid":"tx-plan","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The first time Rue saw the Mercy Academy close up, it was tighter than the pictures had suggested: a band of pale wall against the sky, glasshouses like ribs, and a low harbor crowded with lighters that smelled of salt and coal. She came in winter, with her thin cloak buttoned against wind that knew the island's name and spat it out. The Great Hall stood with its doors open like a mouth of hospitality; under the portico the Headmistress waited in a collar that was more law than ornament. She smiled as if she had shown that smile before and found it useful.\n\n“One hundred this year,” the Headmistress said when the ledger was handed over. “One hundred and none wasted.”\n\nThey read the names aloud. The Folio lay on a dais, its binding dark with old oils and the hands of scribes; the voice that read the names had the patient cadence of someone who had watched girls become a rhythm. Amber light stained the pages where ink had soaked into leather. An Amber Bell hung by a silver hook; when it rang the sound filled the Hall and closed the bargain, a neat note of sound that said both welcome and sealing. Rue had come with a purse that held the price of a clause and a will that weighed less than her own need. She came because her mother was ill and her brothers' debts were songs that would not stop, and because there was a phrase on the small handbill one of the lighters had given her that said Mercy Academy: refuge, education, honourable placement. The phrase had fit a long way into the hollow where hope sat.\n\nShe signed the Contract in a clean hand that trembled at the end. It promised education, shelter, apprenticeship, the learning of trades and the promise of a place to stand after ten years. The margins, as the Academy’s lawyer later explained, were for technicalities. “We cannot take everyone,” he said, sliding a pamphlet across the table. The pamphlet set the year’s cohort at exactly one hundred girls, explained the Academy’s charitable charter, and listed the civic patrons who kept the island alive. The Headmistress nodded; her voice made the island’s mercies sound like civic virtue.\n\n“You will be safe. You will learn. In ten years—” she looked at Rue the way one inspects a document, “—three have returned. Three is our record, and they speak for what we have been able to do.”\n\nRue put her thumb to the wax that the scribe pressed into the Contract. The Binding Seal smelt of beeswax and a bitter iron tang, a careful scent like a first prayer. She heard the faint click of ink against vellum and something like a coil unbent in the basement of the Academy, and for a second she saw the ledger it would write on, not yet open to her name. She paid the purse that the procurer asked for, the money taken from the little savings she had scraped, and the sea took the last of her ordinary life and boiled it down.\n\nAfter the bell she walked the gardens in a kind of disbelief. The Academy was, insofar as the city believed anything, a place where girls were taught to stitch and to read books, to prune roses and to handle good clients at the patron tables. Children left with needles and numbers, with an ability to stand in the world and be usefully womaned. The Headmistress’s speeches said “rescue” and “empowerment” and the city paper printed them obediently. But there were things they said as if they were only proper to be heard in a quiet room: that the Folio recorded both admission and leaving, and that names put in it were not a promise but a ledger—legal things of paper given force by the Seal.\n\nOn the first night the Hundred were assigned to rooms that smelled of lavender and damp stone. Rue shared a low bed with Aya, a girl thinner than her who smiled at Rue until the smile became familiar and then necessary. Aya talked too fast and laughed at the wrong times and knew how to hide a bread crust wrapped in a rag in the hems of her skirt. “I came because my father told me married would be worse,” she said, leaning toward Rue as if they were conspiring. They lay awake counting their bargains. The Amber Bell tolled once again, a private echo in the dormitory that belonged to the older girls.\n\nThere were lessons every day: the right way to hold a needle, the right word to say when a patron asked how your mother was, the scriptures the Academy thought proper even if they were more civic than holy. There were also tasks that no brochure mentioned—ledgers to fill, small clerical pains that sharpened fingers and blurred clocks. In the Ink Room Rue saw the Folio at close range: its pages turned with ceremonious care, the names already written in columns that drew the life the girls now offered into a tidy graph. “We keep things,” an old scribe said without looking up. “We keep them clean.”\n\nMonths became years. Rue learned to mend a winter coat so the stitches did not show; she learned to make a stew that could be plated in a patron’s hall; she learned to read the Folio with a kind of practitioner’s eye. The Binding Seal was explained by rote: it anchored a contract to the Academy and, through the Seal’s ritual, bound an obligation to the ledger. It was not, the instructors insisted, a prison. “Only three have left,” Loren, Rue’s teacher in craft and discipline, reminded the girls. He was not married to the Academy with ribboned speeches; he taught with a dry touch and an honest face. “Three is not nothing. Three is—” he paused, and his look made it clear he accepted the number as both miracle and indictment.\n\nRue kept waiting for the day when the promise of ten years became the promise of a life outside the walls. She’d told herself she would leave the Academy with skills as fine and useful as a new dress. She would send money home, help her mother; she would set small lives right. She had not considered that the ten years might be a crucible designed to change people until they did not want out, or that the contract’s fine print could carry an aftertaste of iron.\n\nIn the Ink Room, late one evening, Rue found a ledger with pages discoloured by centuries of ink. It was catalogued not for public view. The Archive Key was small and iron-worn and when she took it to the cabinet a scribe looked at her with something like pity. “You don’t need to be here,” he said. He closed the door behind her and she saw, on a shelf under dust, a stack of old Contracts. One’s ink had faltered at the margin, and a note in a handwriting that might have belonged to an earlier Headmistress mentioned “tethering.”\n\nThe clause read like a promise made to itself: that care might sometimes require impermanent sacrifices, that the Academy’s work asked not only for learning but for a period of binding, in order that the ledger could be balanced. It spoke of names given in exchange—that the Folio recorded departures only when an exchange of names or obligations was accomplished. It was written in the dry voice of bookkeeping and the furtive tone of a person making a calculation in the night. Rue felt the cold of something under her ribs: when she had signed, she had known she was paying with coin. She had not thought she might have paid with a tether she could not see.\n\nYears folded. Aya married the Academy in its particular way—she took a post in the herbarium and never left on the edge of ten years; she told Rue later, in a voice that broke, that she had seen the city from a window once and had turned back to her work, and though she did not say the word, Rue heard “bound” in the way she said “work.” Loren grew older and kept teaching. The Academy became Rue's life by slow accretion. She taught the new Hundred—girls who arrived with the same emptiness and the same clutch of papers at their throats. Sometimes, at dusk, she would open the Folio and run her finger down the list of names, looking for the ones who had left. The Three were three thin paragraphs in the Academy’s public history: Elaine, Maris, Sal. Each had left in a different season, each with a story the Headmistress liked to tell as moral. Rue memorized their names as one remembers the names of saints or storms.\n\nDecades changed Rue’s hands from soft to callused. Her hair stayed dark long enough for the Academy to call her “mature” and “steady.” She rose to be an instructor, and with position came complicity. She told girls sternly to be grateful; she told girls to practice their stitches until they did not hurt. She told herself she had learned to give value for value. When she taught the ritual of sealing a Contract—how to place your signature, how to touch wax, how to stand while the Bind was closed—she felt, under her skin, the old price she had paid. The Headmistress continued to smile as if the smile was a civic effectuality. Under the skins of the younger girls, she saw the same hunger she had carried as a child.\n\nThe first news of the war came in the form of a dispatch boat, and with it a man whose cloak had the smell of iron-smoke and the tiredness of border roads. The War Envoy stepped onto the Academy’s wharf as if he expected to be refused and then was surprised he was not. He sat in the Great Hall and spoke without malice and without needless brittleness. “We are at the gates,” he said. “We do not ask for the Academy to choose sides, only for it to be useful.” His tone suggested that usefulness might take the form of bounty, of shelter, of recruits. The Headmistress replied with the phrasing the Academy had grown expert in: neutrality, humanitarian shelter, safe harbor. She offered the Academy’s storerooms and its kitchens. She parried the Envoy’s look with assurance that the Academy could be a place of civic service.\n\nRue listened from the back. The Academy’s languages—rescue, charity, education—sounded suddenly thin. They were good words, but the world outside had other words. The Envoy’s calmness was not a kindness; it was a ledger. He did not threaten loudly. He did not have to. He had the force of courts behind him and the mathematics of siegecraft. “We will honor the Folio,” he said. “We will honor deeds. We will not see your sanctuary burn unnecessarily.”\n\nAfter the Envoy left the gardens smelled of a different kind of iron. Some students wanted to bargain with him—parade the Academy’s virtue and ask for charted protection under the war’s banners. Others wanted to refuse any external hand. The Headmistress gathered the older instructors in the Great Hall and turned her face, which was not unkind, toward the problem of survival. Her mind worked in careful arithmetic. She knew the city’s magistrates, the cost of bread beneath siege, and the way to make an envoy think your place was a civic resource instead of a familiar to be picked clean.\n\nThen someone the Academy had not expected stepped across the threshold: one of the Three returned. Elaine’s hair had grown white at the temples and she walked with a scar across her throat like a geography of memory. She came back not as the Headmistress’s emboldened success story but as a bearer of a different report: the city beyond the Academy was hungry, its promises dry as bone, and the Academy was not always a mercy so much as a mechanism for shifting burdens.\n\n“I left,” Elaine said at the gathering, “and I saw trade routes burned and promises eaten. I saw what the Academy sent in exchange for departures.” Her voice was steady; she named no names, but the way she let the sentence hang made the Headmistress’s eyes shadow. “There are places where a name being released requires a debt taken. There are places that ask for blood in exchange for passage.”\n\nThe Great Hall went cold as if someone had opened a door to a winter room. Rue felt the old ledger move in the air, a draft from an unopened cabinet. The Headmistress’s face, previously a wall of hospitality, showed flash circuits of resolve. She did not deny that the Folio held exchanges; she reinterpreted them as necessary, as painful and clean. “Three have returned,” she said. “Three have returned because the Academy can make difficult trades.”\n\nThe war taught the Academy that nowhere is an island. When the first barges were set on fire and the harbor’s patrols counted losses, the island’s wall felt thinner. The Envoy’s language sharpened: the war could come close enough to make the Academy’s neutrality a paper shield. He asked, in a way that resembled bookkeeping, for the Academy’s ledgered goods—stores, sanctuaries, perhaps, recruits for the front. The Headmistress, pragmatic and fatalistic, made a choice that she thought would keep the Academy alive. She offered certain stores and a handful of names—names not yet recorded as departures, names she thought the city could spare in defense—if the Envoy would promise restraint and honor.\n\nRue could not reconcile the trade: she had taught that the Academy kept girls safe, that the Bind was a temple of careful law. But she also knew the Folio’s ledgering: names were not abstract, they were exchangeable. She had seen those exchanges in the Archives, written in cramped ink when the city demanded a sacrifice here and the Academy had accounted for it there. The Binding Seal was not merely ink and wax; it was a practice of reciprocity with teeth.\n\nWhen the first mortar thundered and the island’s harbors filled with smoke, the Academy’s defenses were tested. The Seal’s rituals were performed in the Ink Room with the kind of mechanical reverence apprenticeship had taught for decades. They had men in the tower, with ladders and rope and nets and oil. The Amber Bell was rung to mark each closure and each departure—its clang a sound of braiding and of finality. The Hundred did what they had been trained to do: they sheltered, they stitched, they fed, but under the shelter lay a history of people traded and names switched. The war pulled those names forward like a hand uncoiling.\n\nWhen the Folio was opened to the center of the Ink Room, it did not lie. It listed names and dates and the thin, bureaucratic language of exits. But when Rue looked closer—when she pried with the Archive Key and the slow patience of someone who had read the ledger for years—the Folio yielded notes in margins, crossed entries, and a faint, almost-erasured ledger of obligations. The Binding Seal—wax and iron and carefully mixed tincture—had a price. It tethered in a way that made leaving costly. It required duties to be paid. The Three had each left because of different exchanges; Elaine had spoken of blood debts, Maris had left by a patron's favour that could not be replicated, and Sal—who rarely returned—had left because she bore confidences the Academy could barter.\n\nThe war made those debts material. The Envoy wanted names in a way the city’s magistrates did not; he wanted to shape the population with the same lightness the Academy had used in its earlier accounting. Rue found herself at the center in a way she had not expected. She had been inside long enough to stand in the place between memory and procurement. She had a ledger’s memory and a teacher’s hands. If the Academy could write lines in ink, she could read their consequences. If the Folio held the power to bind, the Seal’s mechanics were on the page: it took kinds of obligations and returned kinds of passage. There was no miracle described, only practice.\n\nThere are no easy endings in libraries where the books were written by committees and by desperate hands. Rue understood, finally, that the life she had chosen—the life she had bought with coin and will—was not a free thing to be carried like a possession; it was a part of the academy’s economy. The war asked her to account. The Headmistress accounted too, and in her accounting she made a choice the younger instructors did not like: she would trade a number of unrecorded claims for passage, and she would tie certain girls to the city’s defense in a way that made them instruments rather than apprentices.\n\nRue could have accepted the arithmetic. She could have kept her place, taken her wage, and taught the next Hundred how to make practical lives of their bindings. Instead she walked to the Ink Room and asked for the Archive Key. She sat with the Folio and the Seal and the looping, patient ink of the scribe. She read every clause that had been inked, every margin note, every old signature. Then she did something the Headmistress had expected all along by the way she had taught Rue to be precise: she made a ledger of her own.\n\nIt was not a miracle. It was a ledger entry. Rue found ways to redraw exchanges by naming obligations aloud, by making tender, evident trades that could be witnessed. She called on the old scribe’s sense of duty, on the apprentices’ loyalty, on Loren's clear sense of fairness. She negotiated with the War Envoy in the language he respected: accounting. She promised—she traded—what the Academy truly had: the method of the Bind itself, recorded honestly, with all its costs. She proposed that if the Envoy and the city took only from the Academy what the Academy could show it had clear, honest obligations to, then fewer names would be taken by stealth and more lives would be preserved with choice.\n\nIt was an ugly calculus and it would mean loss. Rue did not imagine a world where every binding was undone. She knew as well as the scribe who had taught her that ledgering can only shift weight, not deny gravity. But in the act of making the Folio honest, she found a way to let some leave because they had properly paid or because an obligation had been transferred in the light of witnesses. The War Envoy was not moved by morality but by arithmetic: he accepted what could be accounted for.\n\nIn the years after the smoke cleared, the island did not return to what it had been. The Academy’s ledger was altered. It listed more departures with more honest margins. There were fewer dark notes of \"untendered exchange\" and more careful paragraphs of account. Rue lived to see the Folio open to names she had helped untether. The Three were no longer a mythic triumvirate but a set of stories with clearer edges; Elaine, who had returned to tell the truth, left again on terms that did not hide their cost. Maris took a patron’s favor with a clear bill of sale. Sal, who left with secrets, left under witness instead of stealth.\n\nRue’s last days were not dramatic. She taught less and sat by the greenhouses more. Girls passed her with small thanks. She opened the Folio sometimes and thought of the coin she had paid when she was young and cold. She had wrested from the Academy’s accounting not a full forgiveness but a kind of integrity. That was something—an echo rather than a repair. The Amber Bell still rang when the ledger closed a year’s entries, and the sound had lost none of its power. It had shifted, the way a bell’s ring shifts when the metal is tempered differently. Rue had kept her life inside and reshaped what that life had been worth.\n\nWhen she finally left—if leaving for an old woman can be called such—she did so in the public record as part of an exchange the Academy could stand behind. She walked past the glasshouses and the harbor and did not tremble. She had sold herself when she was young, and in the selling she had been given years that kept her mother alive and that taught Rue the needle and the ledger. She had not been given everything. But in the last calculations she had learned to be precise in trade and human enough to make the trade matter.\n\nOutside, the city smelled differently; bronze work glinted in a sun that had its own mathematics. The war had not been entirely merciful, and the island had paid as any place must. But Rue walked with a record under her arm—the legal, honest kind—and a small satisfaction that the ledger she had once signed with a youthful certainty was now, at last, more true. The Mercy Academy still called itself mercy, and the word still had the sharpened edge of economy. Rue had learned to live in that space: not to accept the Academy’s easiest version of itself, nor to tear it down in a single night, but to force the books into light so that choice, however begrudging, might have room.\n\nIn the Folio, later scribes would write Rue’s name carefully. The Amber Bell would ring for her exit. Some would call her a renegade, others a hero. The Headmistress would say, in public, that the Academy had changed for the better. Rue did not expect any single story to be true to every life. She thought of the Hundred, of the girls who came in with pockets light and mouths full of names they trusted: she thought of Aya, who had married the herbarium and who came to Rue in the end with eyes wet and hands that smelled of herbs. She thought of the Three, whose departures had been counted as miracles and warnings. She had been one of the Academy’s young bargains; she had grown older inside it; she had, finally, used the craft the Academy had given her to alter what the Academy had always done.\n\nWhen the last line of ink dried in the ledger that recorded her departure, a scribe closed the Folio with a sure hand. The Amber Bell was rung, and the sound was not the same as it had been years earlier. ./runtime/transcripts/orchestrator/run-2026-07-27T13-32-39-368Z.jsonl:8:{"at":"2026-07-27T13:36:42.197Z","txid":"tx-plan","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The first time Rue saw the Mercy Academy close up, it was tighter than the pictures had suggested: a band of pale wall against the sky, glasshouses like ribs, and a low harbor crowded with lighters that smelled of salt and coal. She came in winter, with her thin cloak buttoned against wind that knew the island's name and spat it out. The Great Hall stood with its doors open like a mouth of hospitality; under the portico the Headmistress waited in a collar that was more law than ornament. She smiled as if she had shown that smile before and found it useful.\n\n“One hundred this year,” the Headmistress said when the ledger was handed over. “One hundred and none wasted.”\n\nThey read the names aloud. The Folio lay on a dais, its binding dark with old oils and the hands of scribes; the voice that read the names had the patient cadence of someone who had watched girls become a rhythm. Amber light stained the pages where ink had soaked into leather. An Amber Bell hung by a silver hook; when it rang the sound filled the Hall and closed the bargain, a neat note of sound that said both welcome and sealing. Rue had come with a purse that held the price of a clause and a will that weighed less than her own need. She came because her mother was ill and her brothers' debts were songs that would not stop, and because there was a phrase on the small handbill one of the lighters had given her that said Mercy Academy: refuge, education, honourable placement. The phrase had fit a long way into the hollow where hope sat.\n\nShe signed the Contract in a clean hand that trembled at the end. It promised education, shelter, apprenticeship, the learning of trades and the promise of a place to stand after ten years. The margins, as the Academy’s lawyer later explained, were for technicalities. “We cannot take everyone,” he said, sliding a pamphlet across the table. The pamphlet set the year’s cohort at exactly one hundred girls, explained the Academy’s charitable charter, and listed the civic patrons who kept the island alive. The Headmistress nodded; her voice made the island’s mercies sound like civic virtue.\n\n“You will be safe. You will learn. In ten years—” she looked at Rue the way one inspects a document, “—three have returned. Three is our record, and they speak for what we have been able to do.”\n\nRue put her thumb to the wax that the scribe pressed into the Contract. The Binding Seal smelt of beeswax and a bitter iron tang, a careful scent like a first prayer. She heard the faint click of ink against vellum and something like a coil unbent in the basement of the Academy, and for a second she saw the ledger it would write on, not yet open to her name. She paid the purse that the procurer asked for, the money taken from the little savings she had scraped, and the sea took the last of her ordinary life and boiled it down.\n\nAfter the bell she walked the gardens in a kind of disbelief. The Academy was, insofar as the city believed anything, a place where girls were taught to stitch and to read books, to prune roses and to handle good clients at the patron tables. Children left with needles and numbers, with an ability to stand in the world and be usefully womaned. The Headmistress’s speeches said “rescue” and “empowerment” and the city paper printed them obediently. But there were things they said as if they were only proper to be heard in a quiet room: that the Folio recorded both admission and leaving, and that names put in it were not a promise but a ledger—legal things of paper given force by the Seal.\n\nOn the first night the Hundred were assigned to rooms that smelled of lavender and damp stone. Rue shared a low bed with Aya, a girl thinner than her who smiled at Rue until the smile became familiar and then necessary. Aya talked too fast and laughed at the wrong times and knew how to hide a bread crust wrapped in a rag in the hems of her skirt. “I came because my father told me married would be worse,” she said, leaning toward Rue as if they were conspiring. They lay awake counting their bargains. The Amber Bell tolled once again, a private echo in the dormitory that belonged to the older girls.\n\nThere were lessons every day: the right way to hold a needle, the right word to say when a patron asked how your mother was, the scriptures the Academy thought proper even if they were more civic than holy. There were also tasks that no brochure mentioned—ledgers to fill, small clerical pains that sharpened fingers and blurred clocks. In the Ink Room Rue saw the Folio at close range: its pages turned with ceremonious care, the names already written in columns that drew the life the girls now offered into a tidy graph. “We keep things,” an old scribe said without looking up. “We keep them clean.”\n\nMonths became years. Rue learned to mend a winter coat so the stitches did not show; she learned to make a stew that could be plated in a patron’s hall; she learned to read the Folio with a kind of practitioner’s eye. The Binding Seal was explained by rote: it anchored a contract to the Academy and, through the Seal’s ritual, bound an obligation to the ledger. It was not, the instructors insisted, a prison. “Only three have left,” Loren, Rue’s teacher in craft and discipline, reminded the girls. He was not married to the Academy with ribboned speeches; he taught with a dry touch and an honest face. “Three is not nothing. Three is—” he paused, and his look made it clear he accepted the number as both miracle and indictment.\n\nRue kept waiting for the day when the promise of ten years became the promise of a life outside the walls. She’d told herself she would leave the Academy with skills as fine and useful as a new dress. She would send money home, help her mother; she would set small lives right. She had not considered that the ten years might be a crucible designed to change people until they did not want out, or that the contract’s fine print could carry an aftertaste of iron.\n\nIn the Ink Room, late one evening, Rue found a ledger with pages discoloured by centuries of ink. It was catalogued not for public view. The Archive Key was small and iron-worn and when she took it to the cabinet a scribe looked at her with something like pity. “You don’t need to be here,” he said. He closed the door behind her and she saw, on a shelf under dust, a stack of old Contracts. One’s ink had faltered at the margin, and a note in a handwriting that might have belonged to an earlier Headmistress mentioned “tethering.”\n\nThe clause read like a promise made to itself: that care might sometimes require impermanent sacrifices, that the Academy’s work asked not only for learning but for a period of binding, in order that the ledger could be balanced. It spoke of names given in exchange—that the Folio recorded departures only when an exchange of names or obligations was accomplished. It was written in the dry voice of bookkeeping and the furtive tone of a person making a calculation in the night. Rue felt the cold of something under her ribs: when she had signed, she had known she was paying with coin. She had not thought she might have paid with a tether she could not see.\n\nYears folded. Aya married the Academy in its particular way—she took a post in the herbarium and never left on the edge of ten years; she told Rue later, in a voice that broke, that she had seen the city from a window once and had turned back to her work, and though she did not say the word, Rue heard “bound” in the way she said “work.” Loren grew older and kept teaching. The Academy became Rue's life by slow accretion. She taught the new Hundred—girls who arrived with the same emptiness and the same clutch of papers at their throats. Sometimes, at dusk, she would open the Folio and run her finger down the list of names, looking for the ones who had left. The Three were three thin paragraphs in the Academy’s public history: Elaine, Maris, Sal. Each had left in a different season, each with a story the Headmistress liked to tell as moral. Rue memorized their names as one remembers the names of saints or storms.\n\nDecades changed Rue’s hands from soft to callused. Her hair stayed dark long enough for the Academy to call her “mature” and “steady.” She rose to be an instructor, and with position came complicity. She told girls sternly to be grateful; she told girls to practice their stitches until they did not hurt. She told herself she had learned to give value for value. When she taught the ritual of sealing a Contract—how to place your signature, how to touch wax, how to stand while the Bind was closed—she felt, under her skin, the old price she had paid. The Headmistress continued to smile as if the smile was a civic effectuality. Under the skins of the younger girls, she saw the same hunger she had carried as a child.\n\nThe first news of the war came in the form of a dispatch boat, and with it a man whose cloak had the smell of iron-smoke and the tiredness of border roads. The War Envoy stepped onto the Academy’s wharf as if he expected to be refused and then was surprised he was not. He sat in the Great Hall and spoke without malice and without needless brittleness. “We are at the gates,” he said. “We do not ask for the Academy to choose sides, only for it to be useful.” His tone suggested that usefulness might take the form of bounty, of shelter, of recruits. The Headmistress replied with the phrasing the Academy had grown expert in: neutrality, humanitarian shelter, safe harbor. She offered the Academy’s storerooms and its kitchens. She parried the Envoy’s look with assurance that the Academy could be a place of civic service.\n\nRue listened from the back. The Academy’s languages—rescue, charity, education—sounded suddenly thin. They were good words, but the world outside had other words. The Envoy’s calmness was not a kindness; it was a ledger. He did not threaten loudly. He did not have to. He had the force of courts behind him and the mathematics of siegecraft. “We will honor the Folio,” he said. “We will honor deeds. We will not see your sanctuary burn unnecessarily.”\n\nAfter the Envoy left the gardens smelled of a different kind of iron. Some students wanted to bargain with him—parade the Academy’s virtue and ask for charted protection under the war’s banners. Others wanted to refuse any external hand. The Headmistress gathered the older instructors in the Great Hall and turned her face, which was not unkind, toward the problem of survival. Her mind worked in careful arithmetic. She knew the city’s magistrates, the cost of bread beneath siege, and the way to make an envoy think your place was a civic resource instead of a familiar to be picked clean.\n\nThen someone the Academy had not expected stepped across the threshold: one of the Three returned. Elaine’s hair had grown white at the temples and she walked with a scar across her throat like a geography of memory. She came back not as the Headmistress’s emboldened success story but as a bearer of a different report: the city beyond the Academy was hungry, its promises dry as bone, and the Academy was not always a mercy so much as a mechanism for shifting burdens.\n\n“I left,” Elaine said at the gathering, “and I saw trade routes burned and promises eaten. I saw what the Academy sent in exchange for departures.” Her voice was steady; she named no names, but the way she let the sentence hang made the Headmistress’s eyes shadow. “There are places where a name being released requires a debt taken. There are places that ask for blood in exchange for passage.”\n\nThe Great Hall went cold as if someone had opened a door to a winter room. Rue felt the old ledger move in the air, a draft from an unopened cabinet. The Headmistress’s face, previously a wall of hospitality, showed flash circuits of resolve. She did not deny that the Folio held exchanges; she reinterpreted them as necessary, as painful and clean. “Three have returned,” she said. “Three have returned because the Academy can make difficult trades.”\n\nThe war taught the Academy that nowhere is an island. When the first barges were set on fire and the harbor’s patrols counted losses, the island’s wall felt thinner. The Envoy’s language sharpened: the war could come close enough to make the Academy’s neutrality a paper shield. He asked, in a way that resembled bookkeeping, for the Academy’s ledgered goods—stores, sanctuaries, perhaps, recruits for the front. The Headmistress, pragmatic and fatalistic, made a choice that she thought would keep the Academy alive. She offered certain stores and a handful of names—names not yet recorded as departures, names she thought the city could spare in defense—if the Envoy would promise restraint and honor.\n\nRue could not reconcile the trade: she had taught that the Academy kept girls safe, that the Bind was a temple of careful law. But she also knew the Folio’s ledgering: names were not abstract, they were exchangeable. She had seen those exchanges in the Archives, written in cramped ink when the city demanded a sacrifice here and the Academy had accounted for it there. The Binding Seal was not merely ink and wax; it was a practice of reciprocity with teeth.\n\nWhen the first mortar thundered and the island’s harbors filled with smoke, the Academy’s defenses were tested. The Seal’s rituals were performed in the Ink Room with the kind of mechanical reverence apprenticeship had taught for decades. They had men in the tower, with ladders and rope and nets and oil. The Amber Bell was rung to mark each closure and each departure—its clang a sound of braiding and of finality. The Hundred did what they had been trained to do: they sheltered, they stitched, they fed, but under the shelter lay a history of people traded and names switched. The war pulled those names forward like a hand uncoiling.\n\nWhen the Folio was opened to the center of the Ink Room, it did not lie. It listed names and dates and the thin, bureaucratic language of exits. But when Rue looked closer—when she pried with the Archive Key and the slow patience of someone who had read the ledger for years—the Folio yielded notes in margins, crossed entries, and a faint, almost-erasured ledger of obligations. The Binding Seal—wax and iron and carefully mixed tincture—had a price. It tethered in a way that made leaving costly. It required duties to be paid. The Three had each left because of different exchanges; Elaine had spoken of blood debts, Maris had left by a patron's favour that could not be replicated, and Sal—who rarely returned—had left because she bore confidences the Academy could barter.\n\nThe war made those debts material. The Envoy wanted names in a way the city’s magistrates did not; he wanted to shape the population with the same lightness the Academy had used in its earlier accounting. Rue found herself at the center in a way she had not expected. She had been inside long enough to stand in the place between memory and procurement. She had a ledger’s memory and a teacher’s hands. If the Academy could write lines in ink, she could read their consequences. If the Folio held the power to bind, the Seal’s mechanics were on the page: it took kinds of obligations and returned kinds of passage. There was no miracle described, only practice.\n\nThere are no easy endings in libraries where the books were written by committees and by desperate hands. Rue understood, finally, that the life she had chosen—the life she had bought with coin and will—was not a free thing to be carried like a possession; it was a part of the academy’s economy. The war asked her to account. The Headmistress accounted too, and in her accounting she made a choice the younger instructors did not like: she would trade a number of unrecorded claims for passage, and she would tie certain girls to the city’s defense in a way that made them instruments rather than apprentices.\n\nRue could have accepted the arithmetic. She could have kept her place, taken her wage, and taught the next Hundred how to make practical lives of their bindings. Instead she walked to the Ink Room and asked for the Archive Key. She sat with the Folio and the Seal and the looping, patient ink of the scribe. She read every clause that had been inked, every margin note, every old signature. Then she did something the Headmistress had expected all along by the way she had taught Rue to be precise: she made a ledger of her own.\n\nIt was not a miracle. It was a ledger entry. Rue found ways to redraw exchanges by naming obligations aloud, by making tender, evident trades that could be witnessed. She called on the old scribe’s sense of duty, on the apprentices’ loyalty, on Loren's clear sense of fairness. She negotiated with the War Envoy in the language he respected: accounting. She promised—she traded—what the Academy truly had: the method of the Bind itself, recorded honestly, with all its costs. She proposed that if the Envoy and the city took only from the Academy what the Academy could show it had clear, honest obligations to, then fewer names would be taken by stealth and more lives would be preserved with choice.\n\nIt was an ugly calculus and it would mean loss. Rue did not imagine a world where every binding was undone. She knew as well as the scribe who had taught her that ledgering can only shift weight, not deny gravity. But in the act of making the Folio honest, she found a way to let some leave because they had properly paid or because an obligation had been transferred in the light of witnesses. The War Envoy was not moved by morality but by arithmetic: he accepted what could be accounted for.\n\nIn the years after the smoke cleared, the island did not return to what it had been. The Academy’s ledger was altered. It listed more departures with more honest margins. There were fewer dark notes of \"untendered exchange\" and more careful paragraphs of account. Rue lived to see the Folio open to names she had helped untether. The Three were no longer a mythic triumvirate but a set of stories with clearer edges; Elaine, who had returned to tell the truth, left again on terms that did not hide their cost. Maris took a patron’s favor with a clear bill of sale. Sal, who left with secrets, left under witness instead of stealth.\n\nRue’s last days were not dramatic. She taught less and sat by the greenhouses more. Girls passed her with small thanks. She opened the Folio sometimes and thought of the coin she had paid when she was young and cold. She had wrested from the Academy’s accounting not a full forgiveness but a kind of integrity. That was something—an echo rather than a repair. The Amber Bell still rang when the ledger closed a year’s entries, and the sound had lost none of its power. It had shifted, the way a bell’s ring shifts when the metal is tempered differently. Rue had kept her life inside and reshaped what that life had been worth.\n\nWhen she finally left—if leaving for an old woman can be called such—she did so in the public record as part of an exchange the Academy could stand behind. She walked past the glasshouses and the harbor and did not tremble. She had sold herself when she was young, and in the selling she had been given years that kept her mother alive and that taught Rue the needle and the ledger. She had not been given everything. But in the last calculations she had learned to be precise in trade and human enough to make the trade matter.\n\nOutside, the city smelled differently; bronze work glinted in a sun that had its own mathematics. The war had not been entirely merciful, and the island had paid as any place must. But Rue walked with a record under her arm—the legal, honest kind—and a small satisfaction that the ledger she had once signed with a youthful certainty was now, at last, more true. The Mercy Academy still called itself mercy, and the word still had the sharpened edge of economy. Rue had learned to live in that space: not to accept the Academy’s easiest version of itself, nor to tear it down in a single night, but to force the books into light so that choice, however begrudging, might have room.\n\nIn the Folio, later scribes would write Rue’s name carefully. The Amber Bell would ring for her exit. Some would call her a renegade, others a hero. The Headmistress would say, in public, that the Academy had changed for the better. Rue did not expect any single story to be true to every life. She thought of the Hundred, of the girls who came in with pockets light and mouths full of names they trusted: she thought of Aya, who had married the herbarium and who came to Rue in the end with eyes wet and hands that smelled of herbs. She thought of the Three, whose departures had been counted as miracles and warnings. She had been one of the Academy’s young bargains; she had grown older inside it; she had, finally, used the craft the Academy had given her to alter what the Academy had always done.\n\nWhen the last line of ink dried in the ledger that recorded her departure, a scribe closed the Folio with a sure hand. The Amber Bell was rung, and the sound was not the same as it had been years earlier. ./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md:3:The Ceremony Hall smelled of beeswax polish and boiled linen: the kind of clean that announces itself rather than earning quiet trust. Light came through high windows in long, patient bars. The hundred benches were arranged like a small amphitheatre; families sat in the outer rings, sober as undertakers. In the middle, on a low table, lay the Folio and the Contract: the Folio a wide, dark book with a ribbon that had once been more important than it was now; the Contract folded into a small, precise packet, the paper rubbed where hands had touched it for decades.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md:13:When she closed, she laid the policy of the House into a sentence that would follow all our names, and repeated the line that the Folio itself required be heard: "So entered under the charge of the Mercy Academy. Let the Folio stand as record and law. Let those within this house remember that mercy is accounted for by service and attention, not by indulgence." The scribe moved an inkwell with ceremonious care, and the Contract was handed to me.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md:17:The Contract's clause was quiet in the packet but not shy: ten years. The writing named it without flourish — a span not measured in noble phrase but in the clear currency of years. I traced the number with a fingertip as the scribe held the folio steady. Ten years is a ledger entry; it is not a promise of comfort.
./novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-001.md:29:When the bronze note sounded again, it sounded like a clock. The Bell finished the ceremony and put the House back into its ordinary rhythm. I folded the Contract into my pocket the way you fold a receipt for a transaction that you do not plan to return. That night, when I lay in my clean bed for the first time in months, I thought of the Folio's blank lines and the Headmistress's closing line, and I felt the arithmetic of my choice settle down into the room: a tidy sum, a term, and a witness.

./runtime/transcripts/orchestrator/run-2026-07-27T13-32-39-368Z.jsonl:8:{"at":"2026-07-27T13:36:42.197Z","txid":"tx-plan","role":"assistant","content":[{"type":"text","text":"The first time Rue saw the Mercy Academy close up, it was tighter than the pictures had suggested: a band of pale wall against the sky, glasshouses like ribs, and a low harbor crowded with lighters that smelled of salt and coal. She came in winter, with her thin cloak buttoned against wind that knew the island's name and spat it out. The Great Hall stood with its doors open like a mouth of hospitality; under the portico the Headmistress waited in a collar that was more law than ornament. She smiled as if she had shown that smile before and found it useful.\n\n“One hundred this year,” the Headmistress said when the ledger was handed over. “One hundred and none wasted.”\n\nThey read the names aloud. The Folio lay on a dais, its binding dark with old oils and the hands of scribes; the voice that read the names had the patient cadence of someone who had watched girls become a rhythm. Amber light stained the pages where ink had soaked into leather. An Amber Bell hung by a silver hook; when it rang the sound filled the Hall and closed the bargain, a neat note of sound that said both welcome and sealing. Rue had come with a purse that held the price of a clause and a will that weighed less than her own need. She came because her mother was ill and her brothers' debts were songs that would not stop, and because there was a phrase on the small handbill one of the lighters had given her that said Mercy Academy: refuge, education, honourable placement. The phrase had fit a long way into the hollow where hope sat.\n\nShe signed the Contract in a clean hand that trembled at the end. It promised education, shelter, apprenticeship, the learning of trades and the promise of a place to stand after ten years. The margins, as the Academy’s lawyer later explained, were for technicalities. “We cannot take everyone,” he said, sliding a pamphlet across the table. The pamphlet set the year’s cohort at exactly one hundred girls, explained the Academy’s charitable charter, and listed the civic patrons who kept the island alive. The Headmistress nodded; her voice made the island’s mercies sound like civic virtue.\n\n“You will be safe. You will learn. In ten years—” she looked at Rue the way one inspects a document, “—three have returned. Three is our record, and they speak for what we have been able to do.”\n\nRue put her thumb to the wax that the scribe pressed into the Contract. The Binding Seal smelt of beeswax and a bitter iron tang, a careful scent like a first prayer. She heard the faint click of ink against vellum and something like a coil unbent in the basement of the Academy, and for a second she saw the ledger it would write on, not yet open to her name. She paid the purse that the procurer asked for, the money taken from the little savings she had scraped, and the sea took the last of her ordinary life and boiled it down.\n\nAfter the bell she walked the gardens in a kind of disbelief. The Academy was, insofar as the city believed anything, a place where girls were taught to stitch and to read books, to prune roses and to handle good clients at the patron tables. Children left with needles and numbers, with an ability to stand in the world and be usefully womaned. The Headmistress’s speeches said “rescue” and “empowerment” and the city paper printed them obediently. But there were things they said as if they were only proper to be heard in a quiet room: that the Folio recorded both admission and leaving, and that names put in it were not a promise but a ledger—legal things of paper given force by the Seal.\n\nOn the first night the Hundred were assigned to rooms that smelled of lavender and damp stone. Rue shared a low bed with Aya, a girl thinner than her who smiled at Rue until the smile became familiar and then necessary. Aya talked too fast and laughed at the wrong times and knew how to hide a bread crust wrapped in a rag in the hems of her skirt. “I came because my father told me married would be worse,” she said, leaning toward Rue as if they were conspiring. They lay awake counting their bargains. The Amber Bell tolled once again, a private echo in the dormitory that belonged to the older girls.\n\nThere were lessons every day: the right way to hold a needle, the right word to say when a patron asked how your mother was, the scriptures the Academy thought proper even if they were more civic than holy. There were also tasks that no brochure mentioned—ledgers to fill, small clerical pains that sharpened fingers and blurred clocks. In the Ink Room Rue saw the Folio at close range: its pages turned with ceremonious care, the names already written in columns that drew the life the girls now offered into a tidy graph. “We keep things,” an old scribe said without looking up. “We keep them clean.”\n\nMonths became years. Rue learned to mend a winter coat so the stitches did not show; she learned to make a stew that could be plated in a patron’s hall; she learned to read the Folio with a kind of practitioner’s eye. The Binding Seal was explained by rote: it anchored a contract to the Academy and, through the Seal’s ritual, bound an obligation to the ledger. It was not, the instructors insisted, a prison. “Only three have left,” Loren, Rue’s teacher in craft and discipline, reminded the girls. He was not married to the Academy with ribboned speeches; he taught with a dry touch and an honest face. “Three is not nothing. Three is—” he paused, and his look made it clear he accepted the number as both miracle and indictment.\n\nRue kept waiting for the day when the promise of ten years became the promise of a life outside the walls. She’d told herself she would leave the Academy with skills as fine and useful as a new dress. She would send money home, help her mother; she would set small lives right. She had not considered that the ten years might be a crucible designed to change people until they did not want out, or that the contract’s fine print could carry an aftertaste of iron.\n\nIn the Ink Room, late one evening, Rue found a ledger with pages discoloured by centuries of ink. It was catalogued not for public view. The Archive Key was small and iron-worn and when she took it to the cabinet a scribe looked at her with something like pity. “You don’t need to be here,” he said. He closed the door behind her and she saw, on a shelf under dust, a stack of old Contracts. One’s ink had faltered at the margin, and a note in a handwriting that might have belonged to an earlier Headmistress mentioned “tethering.”\n\nThe clause read like a promise made to itself: that care might sometimes require impermanent sacrifices, that the Academy’s work asked not only for learning but for a period of binding, in order that the ledger could be balanced. It spoke of names given in exchange—that the Folio recorded departures only when an exchange of names or obligations was accomplished. It was written in the dry voice of bookkeeping and the furtive tone of a person making a calculation in the night. Rue felt the cold of something under her ribs: when she had signed, she had known she was paying with coin. She had not thought she might have paid with a tether she could not see.\n\nYears folded. Aya married the Academy in its particular way—she took a post in the herbarium and never left on the edge of ten years; she told Rue later, in a voice that broke, that she had seen the city from a window once and had turned back to her work, and though she did not say the word, Rue heard “bound” in the way she said “work.” Loren grew older and kept teaching. The Academy became Rue's life by slow accretion. She taught the new Hundred—girls who arrived with the same emptiness and the same clutch of papers at their throats. Sometimes, at dusk, she would open the Folio and run her finger down the list of names, looking for the ones who had left. The Three were three thin paragraphs in the Academy’s public history: Elaine, Maris, Sal. Each had left in a different season, each with a story the Headmistress liked to tell as moral. Rue memorized their names as one remembers the names of saints or storms.\n\nDecades changed Rue’s hands from soft to callused. Her hair stayed dark long enough for the Academy to call her “mature” and “steady.” She rose to be an instructor, and with position came complicity. She told girls sternly to be grateful; she told girls to practice their stitches until they did not hurt. She told herself she had learned to give value for value. When she taught the ritual of sealing a Contract—how to place your signature, how to touch wax, how to stand while the Bind was closed—she felt, under her skin, the old price she had paid. The Headmistress continued to smile as if the smile was a civic effectuality. Under the skins of the younger girls, she saw the same hunger she had carried as a child.\n\nThe first news of the war came in the form of a dispatch boat, and with it a man whose cloak had the smell of iron-smoke and the tiredness of border roads. The War Envoy stepped onto the Academy’s wharf as if he expected to be refused and then was surprised he was not. He sat in the Great Hall and spoke without malice and without needless brittleness. “We are at the gates,” he said. “We do not ask for the Academy to choose sides, only for it to be useful.” His tone suggested that usefulness might take the form of bounty, of shelter, of recruits. The Headmistress replied with the phrasing the Academy had grown expert in: neutrality, humanitarian shelter, safe harbor. She offered the Academy’s storerooms and its kitchens. She parried the Envoy’s look with assurance that the Academy could be a place of civic service.\n\nRue listened from the back. The Academy’s languages—rescue, charity, education—sounded suddenly thin. They were good words, but the world outside had other words. The Envoy’s calmness was not a kindness; it was a ledger. He did not threaten loudly. He did not have to. He had the force of courts behind him and the mathematics of siegecraft. “We will honor the Folio,” he said. “We will honor deeds. We will not see your sanctuary burn unnecessarily.”\n\nAfter the Envoy left the gardens smelled of a different kind of iron. Some students wanted to bargain with him—parade the Academy’s virtue and ask for charted protection under the war’s banners. Others wanted to refuse any external hand. The Headmistress gathered the older instructors in the Great Hall and turned her face, which was not unkind, toward the problem of survival. Her mind worked in careful arithmetic. She knew the city’s magistrates, the cost of bread beneath siege, and the way to make an envoy think your place was a civic resource instead of a familiar to be picked clean.\n\nThen someone the Academy had not expected stepped across the threshold: one of the Three returned. Elaine’s hair had grown white at the temples and she walked with a scar across her throat like a geography of memory. She came back not as the Headmistress’s emboldened success story but as a bearer of a different report: the city beyond the Academy was hungry, its promises dry as bone, and the Academy was not always a mercy so much as a mechanism for shifting burdens.\n\n“I left,” Elaine said at the gathering, “and I saw trade routes burned and promises eaten. I saw what the Academy sent in exchange for departures.” Her voice was steady; she named no names, but the way she let the sentence hang made the Headmistress’s eyes shadow. “There are places where a name being released requires a debt taken. There are places that ask for blood in exchange for passage.”\n\nThe Great Hall went cold as if someone had opened a door to a winter room. Rue felt the old ledger move in the air, a draft from an unopened cabinet. The Headmistress’s face, previously a wall of hospitality, showed flash circuits of resolve. She did not deny that the Folio held exchanges; she reinterpreted them as necessary, as painful and clean. “Three have returned,” she said. “Three have returned because the Academy can make difficult trades.”\n\nThe war taught the Academy that nowhere is an island. When the first barges were set on fire and the harbor’s patrols counted losses, the island’s wall felt thinner. The Envoy’s language sharpened: the war could come close enough to make the Academy’s neutrality a paper shield. He asked, in a way that resembled bookkeeping, for the Academy’s ledgered goods—stores, sanctuaries, perhaps, recruits for the front. The Headmistress, pragmatic and fatalistic, made a choice that she thought would keep the Academy alive. She offered certain stores and a handful of names—names not yet recorded as departures, names she thought the city could spare in defense—if the Envoy would promise restraint and honor.\n\nRue could not reconcile the trade: she had taught that the Academy kept girls safe, that the Bind was a temple of careful law. But she also knew the Folio’s ledgering: names were not abstract, they were exchangeable. She had seen those exchanges in the Archives, written in cramped ink when the city demanded a sacrifice here and the Academy had accounted for it there. The Binding Seal was not merely ink and wax; it was a practice of reciprocity with teeth.\n\nWhen the first mortar thundered and the island’s harbors filled with smoke, the Academy’s defenses were tested. The Seal’s rituals were performed in the Ink Room with the kind of mechanical reverence apprenticeship had taught for decades. They had men in the tower, with ladders and rope and nets and oil. The Amber Bell was rung to mark each closure and each departure—its clang a sound of braiding and of finality. The Hundred did what they had been trained to do: they sheltered, they stitched, they fed, but under the shelter lay a history of people traded and names switched. The war pulled those names forward like a hand uncoiling.\n\nWhen the Folio was opened to the center of the Ink Room, it did not lie. It listed names and dates and the thin, bureaucratic language of exits. But when Rue looked closer—when she pried with the Archive Key and the slow patience of someone who had read the ledger for years—the Folio yielded notes in margins, crossed entries, and a faint, almost-erasured ledger of obligations. The Binding Seal—wax and iron and carefully mixed tincture—had a price. It tethered in a way that made leaving costly. It required duties to be paid. The Three had each left because of different exchanges; Elaine had spoken of blood debts, Maris had left by a patron's favour that could not be replicated, and Sal—who rarely returned—had left because she bore confidences the Academy could barter.\n\nThe war made those debts material. The Envoy wanted names in a way the city’s magistrates did not; he wanted to shape the population with the same lightness the Academy had used in its earlier accounting. Rue found herself at the center in a way she had not expected. She had been inside long enough to stand in the place between memory and procurement. She had a ledger’s memory and a teacher’s hands. If the Academy could write lines in ink, she could read their consequences. If the Folio held the power to bind, the Seal’s mechanics were on the page: it took kinds of obligations and returned kinds of passage. There was no miracle described, only practice.\n\nThere are no easy endings in libraries where the books were written by committees and by desperate hands. Rue understood, finally, that the life she had chosen—the life she had bought with coin and will—was not a free thing to be carried like a possession; it was a part of the academy’s economy. The war asked her to account. The Headmistress accounted too, and in her accounting she made a choice the younger instructors did not like: she would trade a number of unrecorded claims for passage, and she would tie certain girls to the city’s defense in a way that made them instruments rather than apprentices.\n\nRue could have accepted the arithmetic. She could have kept her place, taken her wage, and taught the next Hundred how to make practical lives of their bindings. Instead she walked to the Ink Room and asked for the Archive Key. She sat with the Folio and the Seal and the looping, patient ink of the scribe. She read every clause that had been inked, every margin note, every old signature. Then she did something the Headmistress had expected all along by the way she had taught Rue to be precise: she made a ledger of her own.\n\nIt was not a miracle. It was a ledger entry. Rue found ways to redraw exchanges by naming obligations aloud, by making tender, evident trades that could be witnessed. She called on the old scribe’s sense of duty, on the apprentices’ loyalty, on Loren's clear sense of fairness. She negotiated with the War Envoy in the language he respected: accounting. She promised—she traded—what the Academy truly had: the method of the Bind itself, recorded honestly, with all its costs. She proposed that if the Envoy and the city took only from the Academy what the Academy could show it had clear, honest obligations to, then fewer names would be taken by stealth and more lives would be preserved with choice.\n\nIt was an ugly calculus and it would mean loss. Rue did not imagine a world where every binding was undone. She knew as well as the scribe who had taught her that ledgering can only shift weight, not deny gravity. But in the act of making the Folio honest, she found a way to let some leave because they had properly paid or because an obligation had been transferred in the light of witnesses. The War Envoy was not moved by morality but by arithmetic: he accepted what could be accounted for.\n\nIn the years after the smoke cleared, the island did not return to what it had been. The Academy’s ledger was altered. It listed more departures with more honest margins. There were fewer dark notes of \"untendered exchange\" and more careful paragraphs of account. Rue lived to see the Folio open to names she had helped untether. The Three were no longer a mythic triumvirate but a set of stories with clearer edges; Elaine, who had returned to tell the truth, left again on terms that did not hide their cost. Maris took a patron’s favor with a clear bill of sale. Sal, who left with secrets, left under witness instead of stealth.\n\nRue’s last days were not dramatic. She taught less and sat by the greenhouses more. Girls passed her with small thanks. She opened the Folio sometimes and thought of the coin she had paid when she was young and cold. She had wrested from the Academy’s accounting not a full forgiveness but a kind of integrity. That was something—an echo rather than a repair. The Amber Bell still rang when the ledger closed a year’s entries, and the sound had lost none of its power. It had shifted, the way a bell’s ring shifts when the metal is tempered differently. Rue had kept her life inside and reshaped what that life had been worth.\n\nWhen she finally left—if leaving for an old woman can be called such—she did so in the public record as part of an exchange the Academy could stand behind. She walked past the glasshouses and the harbor and did not tremble. She had sold herself when she was young, and in the selling she had been given years that kept her mother alive and that taught Rue the needle and the ledger. She had not been given everything. But in the last calculations she had learned to be precise in trade and human enough to make the trade matter.\n\nOutside, the city smelled differently; bronze work glinted in a sun that had its own mathematics. The war had not been entirely merciful, and the island had paid as any place must. But Rue walked with a record under her arm—the legal, honest kind—and a small satisfaction that the ledger she had once signed with a youthful certainty was now, at last, more true. The Mercy Academy still called itself mercy, and the word still had the sharpened edge of economy. Rue had learned to live in that space: not to accept the Academy’s easiest version of itself, nor to tear it down in a single night, but to force the books into light so that choice, however begrudging, might have room.\n\nIn the Folio, later scribes would write Rue’s name carefully. The Amber Bell would ring for her exit. Some would call her a renegade, others a hero. The Headmistress would say, in public, that the Academy had changed for the better. Rue did not expect any single story to be true to every life. She thought of the Hundred, of the girls who came in with pockets light and mouths full of names they trusted: she thought of Aya, who had married the herbarium and who came to Rue in the end with eyes wet and hands that smelled of herbs. She thought of the Three, whose departures had been counted as miracles and warnings. She had been one of the Academy’s young bargains; she had grown older inside it; she had, finally, used the craft the Academy had given her to alter what the Academy had always done.\n\nWhen the last line of ink dried in the ledger that recorded her departure, a scribe closed the Folio with a sure hand. The Amber Bell was rung, and the sound was not the same as it had been years earlier. She smiled as if she had shown that smile before and found it useful.\n\n“One hundred this year,” the Headmistress said when the ledger was handed over. “One hundred and none wasted.”\n\nThey read the names aloud. The Folio lay on a dais, its binding dark with old oils and the hands of scribes; the voice that read the names had the patient cadence of someone who had watched girls become a rhythm. Amber light stained the pages where ink had soaked into leather. An Amber Bell hung by a silver hook; when it rang the sound filled the Hall and closed the bargain, a neat note of sound that said both welcome and sealing. Rue had come with a purse that held the price of a clause and a will that weighed less than her own need. It promised education, shelter, apprenticeship, the learning of trades and the promise of a place to stand after ten years. Three is our record, and they speak for what we have been able to do.”\n\nRue put her thumb to the wax that the scribe pressed into the Contract. The Binding Seal smelt of beeswax and a bitter iron tang, a careful scent like a first prayer. She heard the faint click of ink against vellum and something like a coil unbent in the basement of the Academy, and for a second she saw the ledger it would write on, not yet open to her name.
